title: US Government
description: Free US Government & Civics study guide: 8 units of notes, worked examples, flashcards, and a full practice exam. Completely free.

units.name: Foundations of American Democracy

concepts.intro: The United States was founded on Enlightenment principles of limited government, natural rights, and popular sovereignty.
b: Natural rights: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness (Locke) — government exists to protect them
Popular sovereignty: government's power derives from the consent of the governed
Social contract: people give up some freedom in exchange for ordered liberty and protection of rights
Limited government: government powers are defined and restricted by law (the Constitution)
Declaration of Independence (1776): justified revolution by listing grievances against King George III

concepts.intro: American government blends participatory, pluralist, and elite models of democratic participation.
b: Participatory: broad citizen involvement via referendums, town halls, and initiatives
Pluralist: interest groups compete and bargain to influence policy (Federalist No. 10's faction solution)
Elite: policy is dominated by a small set of wealthy or well-organized actors
The Framers designed a republic (representative democracy), not a direct democracy — filtering popular will through elected bodies
Expansion of suffrage over time: property requirements dropped, then race (15th), gender (19th), poll taxes (24th), age to 18 (26th)

concepts.l: Articles of Confederation and why they failed
concepts.intro: America's first constitution created a weak central government that could not solve national problems.
b: No power to tax — Congress had to request funds from states, which often refused
No executive to enforce laws and no national judiciary to interpret them
Unanimous consent required to amend; 9 of 13 states needed to pass laws
Could not regulate interstate or foreign commerce — states imposed tariffs on each other
Shays' Rebellion (1786–87): armed farmers in Massachusetts exposed the government's inability to maintain order, spurring calls for a stronger union

concepts.l: Drafting the Constitution: compromises at Philadelphia
concepts.intro: The Constitutional Convention of 1787 resolved deep sectional conflicts through landmark compromises.
b: Great Compromise (Connecticut Plan): bicameral Congress — House by population, Senate with equal state representation
Three-Fifths Compromise: enslaved persons counted as three-fifths for both representation and direct taxes
Commerce Compromise: Congress regulates interstate/foreign commerce; no export taxes; slave trade untouched until 1808
Electoral College: indirect election of the president as a compromise between congressional selection and popular vote
Separation of powers + checks and balances distributed federal authority among three branches

concepts.intro: Debate over ratification produced the Constitution's first ten amendments and two enduring political traditions.
b: Federalists (Hamilton, Madison, Jay): strong central government; wrote The Federalist Papers to persuade New York ratification
Anti-Federalists (Patrick Henry, George Mason): feared tyranny of a distant central government; demanded a bill of rights
Federalist No. 10 (Madison): a large republic controls factions better than small democracies
Federalist No. 51: 'If men were angels…' — checks and balances let ambition counteract ambition
Promise of a Bill of Rights secured ratification from key states; first ten amendments added by 1791

keyFacts: Great Compromise = bicameral legislature (House = population, Senate = equal)
Shays' Rebellion exposed Articles of Confederation weakness → Constitutional Convention
Federalist No. 10 = factions | Federalist No. 51 = checks & balances
traps: The Articles of Confederation failed because it was TOO WEAK (no tax/enforce power), not too strong
Anti-Federalists opposed RATIFICATION of the Constitution — not independence from Britain
The Three-Fifths Compromise counted enslaved people for REPRESENTATION AND TAXES — it did not define their humanity

units.name: The Constitution: Principles & Structure

concepts.l: Separation of powers and checks and balances
concepts.intro: Power is divided among three branches, each able to limit the others to prevent tyranny.
b: Legislative makes law, executive enforces it, judiciary interprets it
President can veto bills; Congress can override with two-thirds in both chambers
Senate confirms presidential appointments and ratifies treaties (two-thirds vote)
Congress can impeach and remove federal officials: House impeaches (simple majority), Senate tries (two-thirds to convict)
Judicial review (Marbury v. Madison, 1803) lets courts strike unconstitutional acts

concepts.l: Federalism: division of power between nation and states
concepts.intro: The Constitution splits authority between a national government and the states, evolving over time.
b: Enumerated/delegated powers: listed for Congress in Article I, Section 8 (tax, coin money, declare war, regulate commerce)
Reserved powers: kept by states under the 10th Amendment (education, police powers, elections administration)
Concurrent powers: shared (taxing, building roads, establishing courts)
Necessary and Proper (Elastic) Clause + Supremacy Clause expand federal reach
Dual federalism ('layer cake', pre-1930s) shifted to cooperative federalism ('marble cake') after the New Deal

concepts.l: Landmark Supreme Court cases: federal power
concepts.intro: Key cases established judicial review and broad federal authority.
b: Marbury v. Madison (1803): established judicial review — courts declare acts unconstitutional
McCulloch v. Maryland (1819): upheld implied powers under Necessary and Proper Clause; states cannot tax federal institutions
Gibbons v. Ogden (1824): federal commerce power is supreme over state laws in interstate commerce
United States v. Lopez (1995): first case in 60 years to LIMIT commerce-clause power (Gun-Free School Zones Act struck down)
Citizens United v. FEC (2010): corporate independent political spending is protected speech

concepts.intro: Article V provides two paths to propose and two paths to ratify amendments — deliberately difficult.
b: Proposal: two-thirds of both House and Senate, OR a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures (never used)
Ratification: three-fourths of state legislatures OR three-fourths of state ratifying conventions (used once — 21st Amendment)
27 amendments total; the first ten are the Bill of Rights
Bill of Rights guarantees: speech, religion, press, assembly, petition; bear arms; quartering; search/seizure; due process; jury; cruel/unusual punishment
Reconstruction Amendments: 13th (abolish slavery), 14th (equal protection, due process applies to states), 15th (vote regardless of race)

concepts.l: The Bill of Rights and incorporation
concepts.intro: The 14th Amendment's Due Process Clause extended most Bill of Rights protections to the states.
b: Selective incorporation: the Court applied amendments one-by-one against states (Gitlow v. New York began it, 1925)
Near v. Minnesota (1931): freedom of the press incorporated
Mapp v. Ohio (1961): exclusionary rule incorporated (evidence obtained illegally is inadmissible)
Gideon v. Wainwright (1963): right to counsel in felony cases incorporated
McDonald v. Chicago (2010): Second Amendment right to bear arms incorporated

keyFacts: Marbury v. Madison = judicial review (1803)
10th Amendment = reserved powers to the states
Amendment path: 2/3 proposal + 3/4 ratification
traps: Judicial review came from Marbury v. Madison, NOT from the text of the Constitution itself
Incorporation applies the Bill of Rights to STATES via the 14th Amendment — the original rights only bound the federal government
The Elastic Clause expands CONGRESS's power — it does not grant the president new authority

units.name: Congress

concepts.intro: A bicameral legislature balances population-based and equal state representation.
b: House: 435 members, 2-year terms, must be 25+, apportioned by population; initiates revenue bills and impeachment
Senate: 100 members, 6-year staggered terms, must be 30+; confirms appointments, ratifies treaties, tries impeachments
Reapportionment follows each decennial census; redistricting is done by states (gerrymandering risk)
Baker v. Carr (1962) + Wesberry v. Sanders (1964): 'one person, one vote' — districts must be roughly equal in population
Incumbency advantage: name recognition, casework, franking privileges, PAC donations → ~90% House reelection rates

concepts.intro: Article I grants enumerated legislative powers plus implied authority.
b: Levy taxes, borrow money, coin currency, regulate interstate and foreign commerce
Declare war, raise and fund armies, provide for the common defense
Necessary and Proper Clause stretches enumerated powers into implied ones (McCulloch)
Oversight: committees investigate the executive, subpoena witnesses, control budgets
Impeachment: House charges by simple majority; Senate convicts and removes by two-thirds

concepts.l: How a bill becomes a law
concepts.intro: The legislative process filters proposals through committee, floor action, and conference.
b: Introduction → committee assignment → subcommittee review and markup
Committee can pigeonhole (kill) or report out a bill; discharge petition can force a floor vote
House: Rules Committee sets debate terms; Senate: unlimited debate allows filibuster
Filibuster broken by cloture — 60 senators; budget reconciliation needs only a simple majority
Identical passage in both chambers (or conference committee) → president signs or vetoes; veto overridden by two-thirds

concepts.intro: Party leadership and the committee system organize congressional work.
b: Speaker of the House: presides, assigns bills to committees, second in line to presidency
Senate: Vice President is constitutional president (tie-breaker); President pro tempore is ceremonial; Majority Leader runs the floor
Standing committees: permanent subject-matter bodies where most work happens
Committee chairs chosen by seniority within majority party; majority party holds voting majorities on every committee
Divided government (one party holds White House, another Congress) typically slows legislation and raises shutdown/negotiation stakes

keyFacts: Cloture ends a filibuster = 60 votes in the Senate
House starts revenue bills; Senate confirms judges/treaties
Impeach: House majority | Convict/remove: Senate 2/3
traps: The VICE PRESIDENT presides over the SENATE, not the House; the SPEAKER leads the House
Cloture requires 60 votes — not a simple majority of 51
Committee chairs come from the MAJORITY party, chosen by seniority — not appointed by the president

units.name: The Presidency

concepts.intro: Article II lists the president's core authorities.
b: Commander in chief of the armed forces
Negotiate treaties (Senate ratification, two-thirds) and receive ambassadors
Appoint federal officials, judges, and cabinet secretaries (Senate confirmation)
Grant pardons and reprieves for federal offenses (not impeachment cases)
Take Care Clause: faithfully execute the laws; State of the Union duty to recommend measures

concepts.l: Informal powers and the modern presidency
concepts.intro: Presidents increasingly rely on tools beyond the Constitution's text.
b: Executive orders: directives to agencies with force of law; reversible by courts, Congress, or successors
Executive agreements: international pacts made without Senate ratification (e.g., many trade deals)
Signing statements: president's interpretation when signing a bill; controversial if used to refuse enforcement
Bargaining/bully pulpit: persuasion via media attention, agenda setting, going public
Crisis leadership expands presidential power (e.g., post-9/11 security actions)

concepts.intro: Each branch and the Constitution constrain the executive.
b: Congress overrides vetoes, controls funding (power of the purse), and can impeach
Supreme Court can rule executive actions unconstitutional (Youngstown Sheet & Tube v. Sawyer, 1952 — Truman's steel seizure struck down)
War Powers Resolution (1973): president must notify Congress within 48 hours of military action; withdraw within 60 days without authorization
22nd Amendment: two-term limit (post-FDR)
25th Amendment: succession and disability procedures

concepts.intro: From Washington to today, the office has grown far beyond its 18th-century scope.
b: New Deal era: administrative state expanded executive agencies (SEC, SSA)
Post-WWII: standing military and intelligence apparatus centralized in the executive
Imperial presidency critique (Vietnam/Watergate era): unilateral war-making and secrecy exceed constitutional bounds
Unitary executive theory: president controls entire executive branch; used to justify expansive signing statements and orders
Modern presidents use executive orders more in divided government when Congress is gridlocked

keyFacts: Veto override = 2/3 in BOTH chambers
Treaties need Senate 2/3; executive agreements do NOT
War Powers Act: notify in 48h, exit in 60d without authorization
traps: The president CANNOT pardon someone impeached, and pardons are FEDERAL only — not state crimes
Executive agreements skip Senate ratification but bind only while the president's policy stands — treaties are more durable
Commander-in-chief power does NOT include declaring war — that belongs to Congress

units.name: The Judiciary

concepts.l: Structure of the federal court system
concepts.intro: A three-tier hierarchy culminates in the Supreme Court.
b: District courts (94): trial courts of original jurisdiction — hear cases first, juries decide facts
Courts of appeals (13 circuits): review district court decisions for legal error; no juries
Supreme Court: nine justices; mostly appellate jurisdiction plus narrow original jurisdiction (states, ambassadors)
Judges nominated by the president, confirmed by Senate, serve life tenure during good behavior
Federal questions and diversity cases (different states, >$75k) give federal courts jurisdiction

concepts.l: How the Supreme Court chooses and decides cases
concepts.intro: Certiorari, oral argument, and conference shape outcomes.
b: Rule of four: four justices must agree to grant certiorari before a case is heard
Solicitor general represents the U.S. government; amicus curiae briefs add outside perspectives
Majority opinion sets precedent; concurring opinions agree on result but differ on reasoning; dissents disagree entirely
Stare decisis: courts follow precedent — but the Court does overturn itself (Brown reversing Plessy)
Judicial philosophy: strict constructionism/originalism vs. loose/living-document interpretation

concepts.intro: Courts depend on other branches to function.
b: Congress sets court jurisdiction, number of judges, and budgets
President nominates all federal judges; Senate confirms — appointment politics shape the bench
Congress can amend the Constitution to reverse a judicial interpretation (rare — e.g., 16th Amendment after Pollock)
Implementation depends on executive enforcement and public compliance (Jackson: '[Marshall] has made his decision; now let him enforce it')
Legislation can be rewritten to cure constitutional defects the Court identified

keyFacts: Rule of four grants certiorari
Life tenure = during 'good behaviour'
Original jurisdiction is RARE (states, ambassadors); SCOTUS is mainly appellate
traps: The Supreme Court does NOT hear every appeal — it denies most cert petitions (~7,000 filed, <100 heard)
Judicial review is an IMPLIED power from Marbury — not written in Article III
Dissenting opinions have NO legal force but may guide future reasoning

units.name: Civil Liberties & Civil Rights

concepts.intro: Two religion clauses protect belief and constrain government endorsement.
b: Free Exercise Clause: government cannot burden religious practice without compelling interest (Wisconsin v. Yoder, 1972 — Amish schooling exemption)
Establishment Clause: no official religion or excessive entanglement (Lemon v. Kurtzman test; Kennedy v. Bremerton replaced Lemon, 2022)
Engel v. Vitale (1962): school-sponsored prayer unconstitutional, even if voluntary
Employment Division v. Smith (1990): neutral, generally applicable laws do not violate Free Exercise even if they incidentally burden religion
Religious Freedom Restoration Act (1993): statutory standard restoring strict scrutiny for federal burdens on religion

concepts.intro: Speech protections are strong but not absolute.
b: Unprotected categories: incitement to imminent lawless action (Brandenburg), true threats, obscenity (Miller test), defamation of public figures (actual malice, NYT v. Sullivan)
Symbolic speech protected: Texas v. Johnson (1989) flag burning; Tinker v. Des Moines (1969) student armbands
Prior restraint presumed unconstitutional: Near v. Minnesota; NYT v. United States (Pentagon Papers, 1971)
Time/place/manner restrictions allowed for content-neutral purposes (permits, noise limits)
Hazelwood v. Kuhlmeier (1988): schools may censor school-sponsored newspapers for pedagogical reasons

concepts.l: Second, Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, Eighth Amendments
concepts.intro: Core criminal-procedure and gun-rights protections.
b: District of Columbia v. Heller (2008): individual right to keep a handgun at home; McDonald (2010) applied it to states
Fourth Amendment: warrants require probable cause; exclusionary rule (Mapp) bars illegally seized evidence; automobile/plain-view exceptions exist
Fifth: self-incrimination (Miranda warnings), double jeopardy, grand jury, due process, takings compensation
Sixth: speedy/public trial, impartial jury, notice of charges, confront witnesses, counsel (Gideon)
Eighth: no cruel and unusual punishment; death penalty constitutional with safeguards (Gregg v. Georgia) but barred for minors/intellectually disabled

concepts.intro: An unenumerated right built from amendment 'penumbras.'
b: Griswold v. Connecticut (1965): marital contraception privacy from 1st/3rd/4th/5th/9th/14th amendments
Roe v. Wade (1973): abortion under due process; overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson (2022), returning regulation to states
Lawrence v. Texas (2003): private consensual intimacy protected
Obergefell v. Hodges (2015): same-sex marriage under 14th Amendment equal protection and due process
Privacy debates center on which unenumerated rights survive textualist scrutiny

concepts.intro: The 14th Amendment drives anti-discrimination law.
b: Strict scrutiny: race/national origin classifications — government must show compelling interest and narrow tailoring
Intermediate scrutiny: gender — substantially related to important objective (Craig v. Boren)
Rational basis: most other classifications — rationally related to legitimate goal (almost always upheld)
Brown v. Board (1954): separate is inherently unequal in education; reversed Plessy's separate-but-equal
Affirmative action: permitted with limits — SFFA v. Harvard (2023) ended race-conscious college admissions

keyFacts: Strict scrutiny (race) > intermediate (gender) > rational basis (most)
Heller = individual gun right at home; McDonald = applies to states
Brown reversed Plessy; Dobbs reversed Roe
traps: Free speech does NOT protect incitement, true threats, obscenity, or defamation — 'no shouting fire in a crowded theater'
Miranda warnings are required for CUSTODIAL INTERROGATION — not every police encounter
The Establishment Clause blocks government ENDORSEMENT of religion — it does not ban private religious expression

units.name: Political Participation: Elections & Media

concepts.intro: Parties nominate candidates, mobilize voters, and structure government — despite the Founders' warnings.
b: Party functions: recruit candidates, fundraise, get-out-the-vote, organize Congress by caucus
Party eras: Federalist/Democratic-Republican, Jacksonian Democrats vs. Whigs, Republican ascendancy (1860–1932), New Deal coalition (1932–1968), dealignment/divided government since
Realignment: durable shift in coalitions (e.g., Southern realignment toward Republicans post-Civil Rights Act)
Third parties: winner-take-all plurality (Duverger's law) squeezes minor parties; they still inject new ideas (Populists, Socialists) and act as spoilers
Primaries weakened party bosses: candidate-centered campaigns dominate since McGovern-Fraser reforms (1972)

concepts.intro: Who votes, how, and why turnout varies.
b: Presidential elections: Electoral College — 538 electors, need 270; winner-take-all in 48 states; swing states decide close races
Midterm turnout lags presidential (~40% vs ~60%+); local elections lower still
Predictors of turnout: education, age (older vote more), income; registration barriers suppress turnout
Motor Voter Act (1993): register at DMV; Help America Vote Act (2002): provisional ballots after Bush v. Gore
Voting Rights Act (1965): banned literacy tests, federal preclearance for discriminatory jurisdictions (Shelby County v. Holder gutted preclearance formula in 2013)

concepts.intro: Organized groups shape policy between elections.
b: Methods: lobbying, litigation (amicus briefs, class actions), electioneering, grassroots mobilization
Iron triangles: agency + congressional committee + interest group dominate a policy area; issue networks are looser, broader webs
Free-rider problem: collective goods (clean air) attract non-members who benefit without joining — Olson's logic
Campaign finance: Buckley v. Valeo (1976) — spending is speech; contribution limits OK, expenditure limits suspect
BCRA/McCain-Feingold (2002) softened soft-money rules; Citizens United (2010) opened independent corporate expenditures and super PACs

concepts.intro: Media informs voters and frames politics — with structural biases.
b: Roles: gatekeeping (what gets covered), scorekeeping (polls/horserace), watchdog (investigations — Watergate, Pentagon Papers)
Fragmentation: cable news, talk radio, social media create echo chambers and selective exposure
Horse-race coverage emphasizes who's winning over policy substance
Fairness Doctrine abolished (1987); partisan outlets grew after
Misinformation spreads faster than corrections; platform moderation remains contested (First Amendment binds government, not private platforms)

keyFacts: 270 electoral votes wins; 538 total; swing states pivotal
Duverger's law: plurality winners → two-party systems
Citizens United = independent corporate spending OK; contributions still capped
traps: Winning the POPULAR VOTE does not guarantee the presidency — the Electoral College decides (2000, 2016)
Super PACs may raise unlimited funds for INDEPENDENT expenditures only — direct coordination with candidates is illegal
The First Amendment restricts GOVERNMENT censorship — private social platforms can moderate content freely

units.name: The Bureaucracy & Policy Making

concepts.intro: The executive branch implements law through departments, agencies, and commissions.
b: Cabinet departments (15): State, Treasury, Defense, Justice, etc. — secretary appointed by president, confirmed by Senate
Independent regulatory commissions: FCC, SEC, FTC — bipartisan boards, fixed terms, insulated from removal
Government corporations: USPS, Amtrak — hybrid public/private operation
Independent executive agencies: NASA, EPA, CIA — outside cabinet but report to president
~2 million civilian federal employees; most hired via merit system (Pendleton Act, 1883 ended much of the spoils system)

concepts.intro: Agencies fill in details Congress leaves vague.
b: Congress writes broad statutes; agencies write binding regulations to implement them (notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA)
Discretionary authority: EPA interprets 'harmful pollutant'; IRS defines deductions; FDA approves drugs
Chevron deference (1984): courts deferred to reasonable agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes — overturned by Loper Bright (2024), restoring independent judicial interpretation
Regulations carry force of law once finalized; violations trigger penalties
Rulemaking creates accountability concerns: unelected experts wield significant power

concepts.intro: All three branches plus oversight mechanisms constrain agencies.
b: Congress: passes enabling statutes, controls appropriations, conducts oversight hearings, uses Congressional Review Act to void late-term rules
President: appoints/removes agency heads (except insulated commissioners), issues executive orders, proposes budgets (OMB)
Courts: review agency actions for statutory compliance and constitutional limits
Freedom of Information Act (FOIA): public access to agency records; whistleblower protections expose misconduct
Iron triangle dynamics can capture agencies in industry interests; revolving door fuels critique

concepts.intro: Policy moves through predictable stages from problem to evaluation.
b: Agenda setting: problem recognition, focusing events (crises), media attention, interest group pressure
Formulation: drafting options by think tanks, agencies, congressional staff
Adoption: legislation passed, executive order issued, or regulation finalized
Implementation: agencies translate law into programs; discretion and resources determine fidelity
Evaluation: GAO reports, program reviews feed back into reform — policy feedback loops matter

keyFacts: Notice-and-comment rulemaking = Administrative Procedure Act
Loper Bright (2024) ended Chevron deference
Congressional Review Act voids agency rules by joint resolution
traps: Agencies make REGULATIONS with force of law — but only under authority delegated by CONGRESS's statutes
Independent commission members CANNOT be removed at will by the president (fixed, staggered terms)
The spoils system gave jobs to supporters; the PENDLETON ACT replaced it with merit hiring after Garfield's assassination

quiz.q: Which document justified independence by listing grievances against King George III?
quiz.e: The Declaration of Independence (1776) argued natural rights were violated and dissolved political bonds with Britain.

quiz.q: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could NOT:
quiz.e: Congress could request but not compel tax revenue — the central weakness that doomed the Articles.

quiz.q: Shays' Rebellion convinced many leaders that:
o: A stronger national government was needed
The Bill of Rights was necessary
quiz.e: The 1786 uprising showed the confederation could not maintain domestic order, driving support for the Constitutional Convention.

quiz.q: The Great Compromise resolved disputes over:
quiz.e: It blended the Virginia (population) and New Jersey (equal state) plans into a bicameral legislature.

quiz.q: Federalist No. 10 argued that a large republic:
o: Controls factions better than small democracies
quiz.e: Madison reasoned that diverse interests across a big republic prevent any single faction from dominating.

quiz.q: Anti-Federalists primarily demanded:
quiz.e: Their insistence on explicit rights protections produced the first ten amendments.

quiz.q: 'Consent of the governed' expresses which principle?
quiz.e: Popular sovereignty locates governmental authority in the people themselves.

quiz.q: Judicial review was established by which case?
quiz.e: Chief Justice Marshall's 1803 opinion let courts strike unconstitutional laws.

quiz.q: McCulloch v. Maryland upheld:
o: State power to tax the federal bank
quiz.e: Maryland couldn't tax the Bank; Congress could charter it under the Necessary and Proper Clause.

quiz.q: Powers reserved to the states appear in which amendment?
quiz.e: The Tenth Amendment reserves undelegated powers to states or the people.

quiz.q: Selective incorporation applies Bill of Rights protections to the states through the:
quiz.e: Starting with Gitlow (1925), the Court applied rights one-by-one against the states via the 14th.

quiz.q: To ratify a proposed amendment, three-fourths of what must approve?
quiz.e: Article V requires three-fourths of states via legislatures or conventions.

quiz.q: United States v. Lopez (1995) held that the Gun-Free School Zones Act exceeded:
quiz.e: Possessing a gun near a school wasn't economic activity — a rare commerce-clause limit.

quiz.q: The 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments are collectively called the:
quiz.e: They abolished slavery, guaranteed equal protection/due process, and barred racial voting discrimination.

quiz.q: How many members serve in the Senate?
quiz.e: Two per state × 50 states = 100 senators serving staggered six-year terms.

quiz.q: Revenue (tax) bills must originate in the:
quiz.e: The Origination Clause places taxing bills in the chamber closest to the people.

quiz.q: Ending a filibuster requires:
quiz.e: Cloture needs three-fifths of sworn senators — 60 today.

quiz.q: Convicting and removing an impeached official requires:
quiz.e: The House impeaches by majority; conviction in the Senate needs two-thirds of those present.

quiz.q: The Speaker of the House is chosen by:
quiz.e: The House elects the Speaker — effectively the majority party's leader.

quiz.q: 'One person, one vote' districting came from Baker v. Carr and:
quiz.e: These cases made federal courts referee malapportioned districts.

quiz.q: Most congressional work happens in:
quiz.e: Standing committees screen, amend, and shape nearly all legislation.

quiz.q: Which is a FORMAL presidential power?
quiz.e: Appointment power appears in Article II; orders, bargaining, and party leadership are informal.

quiz.q: Treaties negotiated by the president require:
quiz.e: The Treaty Clause demands two-thirds of present senators.

quiz.q: Youngstown v. Sawyer (1952) ruled that Truman's steel seizure was:
o: Justified by the Take Care Clause
quiz.e: The Court rejected executive seizure absent congressional authorization — a key check.

quiz.q: The War Powers Resolution requires the president to notify Congress within:
quiz.e: And forces withdrawal within 60 days absent congressional authorization.

quiz.q: A president can be removed by:
quiz.e: House impeachment followed by Senate two-thirds conviction removes a president.

quiz.q: Executive agreements differ from treaties because they:
quiz.e: They're sole-executive pacts; easier to make, easier to undo.

quiz.q: The 22nd Amendment limits presidents to:
quiz.e: Adopted after FDR's four elections; two four-year terms max.

quiz.q: The Supreme Court agrees to hear a case when:
quiz.e: The Rule of Four — four votes put a case on the docket.

quiz.q: Federal district courts are courts of:
quiz.e: Trials happen first in district court; appeals go upward.

quiz.q: Federal judges serve:
quiz.e: Article III tenure insulates judges from political pressure.

quiz.q: A concurring opinion:
o: Agrees with outcome but different reasoning
quiz.e: Concurrences join the result while offering separate logic.

quiz.q: Stare decisis means courts:
quiz.e: Respecting precedent stabilizes law — though Brown shows it yields to correction.

quiz.q: Who nominates federal judges?
quiz.e: Presidential nomination plus Senate confirmation fills Article III seats.

quiz.q: Engel v. Vitale (1962) prohibited:
quiz.e: Official, school-composed prayer violates the Establishment Clause even if nominally voluntary.

quiz.q: Texas v. Johnson (1989) protected flag burning as:
quiz.e: Political expression, however offensive, receives First Amendment protection.

quiz.q: The exclusionary rule from Mapp v. Ohio bars:
quiz.e: Evidence obtained violating the Fourth Amendment is inadmissible against the defendant.

quiz.q: Gideon v. Wainwright guaranteed:
quiz.e: States must supply attorneys to defendants who cannot afford them in felonies.

quiz.q: Race-based government classifications face:
quiz.e: Suspect classifications demand a compelling interest pursued by narrowly tailored means.

quiz.q: Brown v. Board of Education (1954):
quiz.e: It reversed Plessy's separate-but-equal doctrine in public education.

quiz.q: Dobbs v. Jackson (2022):
o: Returned abortion regulation to the states
quiz.e: Overturning Roe/Casey left abortion policy to democratic processes in each state.

quiz.q: How many electoral votes are needed to win the presidency?
quiz.e: A majority of 538 electors — 270 — secures victory.

quiz.q: Duverger's law explains why plurality-winner elections produce:
quiz.e: Winner-take-all districts squeeze votes for third parties, entrenching two blocs.

quiz.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965:
o: Banned literacy tests and enabled federal election oversight
quiz.e: Its preclearance regime targeted jurisdictions with histories of discrimination until Shelby County (2013).

quiz.q: An iron triangle consists of:
quiz.e: Mutually reinforcing relationships dominate narrow policy domains.

quiz.q: Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held that:
o: Corporations may make unlimited independent political expenditures
quiz.e: Independent expenditures — not direct contributions — received First Amendment protection, spawning super PACs.

quiz.q: Media 'gatekeeping' refers to:
quiz.e: Editorial choices about coverage shape what the public sees as important.

quiz.q: Compared with presidential-year turnout, midterm turnout is roughly:
quiz.e: Midterms draw ~40% versus ~60%+ in presidential cycles — low-turnout electorates shift outcomes.

quiz.q: The merit-based civil service largely replaced the spoils system via the:
quiz.e: After Garfield's 1881 assassination, the Pendleton Act (1883) professionalized hiring.

quiz.q: Agencies create binding regulations through:
quiz.e: Proposed rules are published, commented on, then finalized with legal force.

quiz.q: Chevron deference required courts to:
o: Accept reasonable agency readings of ambiguous statutes
quiz.e: Loper Bright (2024) overruled Chevron, making judges independently interpret statutes.

quiz.q: Congress can invalidate a recently finalized agency rule through the:
quiz.e: A CRA joint resolution, signed by the president, voids covered rules.

quiz.q: Independent regulatory commissioners:
o: Have fixed staggered terms limiting removal
quiz.e: Insulation from at-will removal protects bipartisan agency independence.

quiz.q: The first stage of the policy cycle is:
quiz.e: Problems must gain attention before formulation and adoption follow.

quiz.q: FOIA primarily enables:
o: Public access to federal agency records
quiz.e: The Freedom of Information Act lets citizens request agency documents, subject to exemptions.

flashcards.d: Government's legitimacy comes from the consent of the governed — power resides in the people.

Powers expressly granted to Congress in Article I, Section 8 (tax, commerce, war, etc.).

Extended Senate debate delaying/blocking a vote; only possible in the Senate.

Power to review lower-court decisions for legal error.
Order accepting a case for review; granted by the Rule of Four.
'Let the decision stand' — courts adhere to precedent for stability.
Binding rationale of the justices in the majority; sets precedent.
'Friend of the court' filing by non-parties offering expertise/perspective.
Debate over whether courts should overturn policy boldly or defer to elected branches.
First Amendment bar on government establishing/endorsing religion.
Protection for religious practice against government burden.
Government blocking publication in advance — presumptively unconstitutional (Pentagon Papers).
Mapp v. Ohio: evidence from illegal searches inadmissible at trial.
Custodial interrogation requires warning of silence/counsel rights.
Highest review tier (race, fundamental rights): compelling interest + narrow tailoring.
14th Amendment mandate that states treat similarly situated people alike.
Unenumerated liberty (Griswold line) covering contraception, marriage, intimacy; abortion returned to states by Dobbs.
538 electors; 270 to win; most states winner-take-all — can diverge from popular vote.
Competitive states deciding close elections; focus of campaigns.
Plurality-rule elections structurally favor two-party systems.
Durable shift in party coalitions after critical elections (1932 New Deal).
Post-Citizens United committee raising unlimited money for independent expenditures only.
Loose, fluid alliance of experts, groups, and officials around a policy issue (vs. iron triangle).
Media's power to choose which events become news.
Departments/agencies implementing law; staffed mostly by merit-hired civil servants.
APA process: publish proposed rule, take comments, issue final binding regulation.
Agency power to choose how to execute vague statutory mandates.
Tight agency-committee-interest-group axis dominating one policy area.

PART_A.q: Which principle holds that government legitimacy derives from the people's consent?
PART_A.e: Popular sovereignty is the Declaration's core claim: governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed.'

PART_A.q: The primary weakness of the Articles of Confederation was that the national government lacked power to:
PART_A.e: Requisitioning state funds failed repeatedly — fiscal weakness crippled defense and debt payment.

PART_A.q: Which compromise created the current Senate structure?
PART_A.e: Equal state representation in the upper chamber came from the Connecticut plan.

PART_A.q: Federalist No. 51 defends which design feature?

PART_A.e: Marbury vested courts with constitutional veto power over acts of the political branches.

PART_A.q: Youngstown (1952) teaches that presidential power is weakest when:
PART_A.e: Justice Jackson's framework: executive claims falter most against congressional disapproval.

PART_A.q: The Rule of Four pertains to:
PART_A.e: Four justices' agreement puts a case on the merits docket.

PART_A.q: Federal appellate courts review:
PART_A.e: Appeals panels correct legal mistakes; no juries sit.

PART_A.q: Which amendment guards against unreasonable searches?
PART_A.e: The Fourth requires probable cause and particularized warrants.

PART_A.q: Miranda warnings attach during:
PART_A.e: Custody plus interrogation triggers the warnings.

PART_A.e: A majority of electors — 270 — decides, regardless of popular totals.

PART_A.e: Winner-take-all rewards broad-tent parties and punishes splinters.

PART_B2.q: Explain how Marbury v. Madison strengthened the judiciary relative to the other branches.
PART_B2.sa: By claiming the authority to review acts of Congress and declare them void, the Court positioned itself as co-equal interpreter of the Constitution. Marshall simultaneously denied the Court immediate power (Marbury's commission) while asserting ultimate constitutional authority — avoiding confrontation with Jefferson while establishing judicial review, the branch's defining power.

PART_B2.q: Using McCulloch v. Maryland, explain how the Necessary and Proper and Supremacy Clauses work together.
PART_B2.sa: McCulloch paired them: Maryland couldn't tax the Second Bank because (1) Congress could charter it under the Necessary and Proper Clause's implied powers — the means being legitimate ends of the enumerated taxing/spending/regulating powers — and (2) the Supremacy Clause made a state tax obstructing a constitutional federal instrument invalid. Together they justify broad federal capacity and shield it from state interference.

PART_B2.q: Describe two ways Congress checks the bureaucracy and evaluate which is more consequential.
PART_B2.sa: (1) Appropriations: agencies need annual funding, giving committees leverage over priorities. (2) Oversight: hearings, subpoenas, and GAO audits expose mismanagement; the CRA can void rules outright. Appropriations is generally more consequential — money denial is immediate and unavoidable, whereas oversight depends on publicity and political will.

PART_B2.q: Explain why third parties struggle under U.S. election rules, citing a specific mechanism.
PART_B2.sa: Single-member districts with plurality winners (first-past-the-post) mean votes for minor parties rarely translate into seats — Duverger's law. Ballot-access laws, debate-exclusion thresholds, and matching-funds rules add hurdles. The 1992 Perot campaign illustrates the ceiling: 19% popular vote, zero electoral votes.

PART_B2.q: Compare strict scrutiny and rational basis review, and explain why the difference decides outcomes.
PART_B2.sa: Strict scrutiny (race, fundamental rights) puts the burden on government to prove a compelling interest achieved by narrow tailoring — almost always fatal. Rational basis asks only whether a classification is rationally related to a legitimate goal — almost always upheld. Intermediate (gender) sits between. Because the burden of proof and the required fit differ so sharply, the choice of tier usually predetermines the result.

PART_B2.q: Explain the tension between the commander-in-chief power and Congress's declaration-of-war power.
PART_B2.sa: The president directs military operations once initiated; only Congress authorizes war. Presidents increasingly engage forces without declarations (Korea, Vietnam, Libya), provoking the War Powers Resolution's 48-hour notice and 60-day limits. Courts avoid the clash (political question), leaving the balance to interbranch contest — hence recurring constitutional controversy.

PART_B2.q: Using Engel v. Vitale and Wisconsin v. Yoder, distinguish the Establishment and Free Exercise Clauses.
PART_B2.sa: Engel enforces the Establishment Clause: government may not compose and sponsor prayer in public schools, protecting conscience from state religion. Yoder enforces Free Exercise: the state's compulsory-attendance interest yielded to Amish religious practice after the eighth grade. One clause restrains government endorsement; the other shields believer conduct from government interference.

PART_B2.q: Explain how the Electoral College can produce a president who lost the popular vote, and identify two elections illustrating this.
PART_B2.sa: Statewide winner-take-all allocation awards all electors to the plurality winner in 48 states; small margins in large swing states therefore swing hundreds of electors while national vote totals differ. 2000 (Bush v. Gore) and 2016 illustrate presidents winning the Electoral College while trailing nationally.

PART_B2.q: Assess ONE argument for and ONE against judicial activism.
PART_B2.sa: For: courts protect discrete and insular minorities when majoritarian branches fail — Brown exemplifies constitutional conscience correcting democracy. Against: unelected justices overriding legislatures lacks democratic warrant and invites countermobilization; critics point to Lochner-era economics or Dobbs-era whiplash as instability caused by aggressive review.

PART_B2.q: Explain why Loper Bright's rejection of Chevron deference changes bureaucratic power.
PART_B2.sa: Under Chevron, ambiguity in statutes defaulted to the administering agency's reasonable reading — a power multiplier for expert bureaus. Loper Bright transfers interpretive finality to courts, shrinking agency discretion, increasing litigation risk for regulated entities and agencies, and pushing Congress to legislate with more specificity if it wants its intent honored.

PART_C.q: 'The Constitution was engineered less for democracy than for controlling factions.' Evaluate this claim using evidence from the founding design.
PART_C.sa:
Supporting evidence: Federalist No. 10's faction theory; filtering choice through the Electoral College and originally state-chosen Senators; separation of powers fragmenting majorities; an unelected judiciary; amendment difficulty. Counter-evidence: the House's direct election, broad suffrage expansion by amendment, and Bill of Rights responsiveness show popular elements and adaptability. Best verdict: the design channels and slows popular will — republican rather than purely democratic — aiming at filtered consensus rather than faction suppression alone.

Scoring (1–2 pts): 1 pt for accurate mechanism(s) with examples; 2nd pt for balanced evaluation acknowledging both design-for-control and democratic features.

PART_C.q: Evaluate whether the modern presidency has grown too powerful relative to Congress, using at least three pieces of evidence.
PART_C.sa:
Evidence for growth: standing military and intelligence under sole executive direction; executive orders/agreements substituting for legislation and treaties; OMB budget dominance; unitary-executive theories expanding removal and secrecy claims. Evidence for continued constraint: appropriation leverage, confirmation chokepoints, Youngstown-style judicial pushback, and divided-government gridlock. Conclusion: power has migrated decisively to the White House in foreign affairs and security policy while domestic policy remains contested — the imbalance is real but branch-dependent.

Scoring (1–2 pts): 1 pt for three accurate evidentiary items; 2nd pt for a defensible evaluative thesis engaging counterarguments.
